analysis.one_liner: Guarantees college athletes the right to be paid for use of their name, image, and likeness.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in committee with zero cosponsors and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar universities and college sports governing bodies like the NCAA from stopping current or future college athletes from being paid for use of their name, image, or likeness. It would also ban schools from coordinating to cap athlete pay, protect athletes' right to hire agents and form collective representatives, require schools and conferences to get a license and disclose revenue before using a group of athletes in promotions, and protect scholarships from being cut because an athlete earns outside money. It would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, private lawsuits, and automatic antitrust liability, and it would fix visa rules so international college athletes can earn this pay too.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, including high-school recruits and international athletes on student visas, gain the right to market their own name, image, and likeness without losing playing time or scholarship money, to hire agents and lawyers, and to band together for group licensing deals. Athletes in revenue sports like football and basketball would see the largest dollar gains, but the bill's disclosure and nondiscrimination rules aim to extend pay to women and athletes in lower-profile sports.

how_it_helps.text: Bars schools and athletic associations from enforcing any rule preventing college athletes or recruits from marketing their names, images, or likenesses.
Prohibits schools from coordinating with other schools or third parties to limit how much athletes are paid, unless a cap was negotiated with a representative of the athletes.
Guarantees athletes the right to hire agents, financial advisors, and lawyers, and to form or join a collective representative such as a players' association, without losing eligibility.
Requires schools and conferences to obtain a group license and disclose what they earn before using a group of athletes' likenesses in promotions or media deals.
Ensures earning outside compensation cannot reduce or jeopardize an athlete's scholarship.
Makes violations enforceable by the FTC, by private lawsuits with attorney's fees, and as a per se violation of the Sherman Act.
Amends visa rules so international college athletes on F visas can engage in NIL activity and be paid like other athletes without violating their immigration status.
Requires institutional NIL collectives to register with the FTC and report agreements by gender, race, and sport, and bars them from discriminating in who gets deals.

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments would pay, since money now captured through media rights and marketing would have to be shared with or licensed from the athletes who generate it. Schools would also bear the cost of complying with disclosure and nondiscrimination requirements, and some schools have warned that paying athletes could squeeze funding for non-revenue sports.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state NIL laws, so states that wrote their own athlete compensation rules would lose the ability to enforce them.
Automatic Sherman Act liability for any violation exposes schools and associations to antitrust damages, which could push universities toward treating athletes as employees with unpredictable costs.

Removing all limits on coordinated pay rules could accelerate a recruiting arms race concentrated in football and basketball, and athletic departments have argued the resulting costs could force cuts to non-revenue sports such as Olympic sports.
The bill authorizes spending on annual market-analysis grants with no dollar limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the athletes affected, the gains are concrete: the right to be paid for a valuable personal asset, to keep scholarships while doing it, and to organize collectively. The costs fall almost entirely on college sports institutions and the conferences that negotiate billion-dollar media contracts, not on taxpayers, though the bill's broad antitrust exposure and preemption of state laws are real design choices an honest supporter would defend rather than deny. The bill is narrow in scope, which limits both its benefits to the general public and its downside.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee, where it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the bill in the Senate on July 26, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote is recorded in the bill's action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments are better off, because the current system in which they license and sell athletes' names, images, and likenesses without a federal right to pay remains intact. State laws, not a uniform federal right, still govern what athletes can earn.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: NCAA, athletic conferences, and college athletic departments

for.name: Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College Athlete Economic Freedom Act and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without any action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: NCAA and member conferences
against.what_they_did: The NCAA has publicly sought Congress to write NIL rules that preserve its authority over athlete compensation rather than bar it, and the college sports industry opposed legislation removing associations' power to cap athlete pay.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so the bill's support never grew beyond a single Democratic sponsor and its partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.industry: NCAA, athletic conferences, and college sports governing bodies
industries.note: The bill would strip these bodies of their power to limit what athletes can earn and make any violation an automatic antitrust violation, transferring money from media-rights and marketing revenue to athletes. Under current law they keep that authority, which is what happened when the bill died.

industries.industry: University athletic departments and college sports media partners
industries.note: Schools and conferences would have to license group athlete likenesses and disclose their revenue from media and promotions before using them, sharing revenue they currently capture. This is the industry side of the roughly billion-dollar college sports media economy.

industries.industry: Sports agents, athlete agencies, and marketing firms
industries.note: The bill guarantees athletes the right to professional representation and bars schools from certifying or restricting agents, expanding the market for athlete representation services.

The bill treats collectives as affiliated with the schools they support, requires FTC registration and annual reporting disaggregated by gender, race, and sport, and bars discriminatory deal facilitation, but leaves them operating as the funding channel for athlete pay.
